{{Orphan|date=July 2024}}

'''Franz Lucretius Gross''' (born August 9, 1937, in [[Minneapolis]]) is an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]].

==Education and career==
Gross studied at [[Swarthmore College]] (Bachelor's degree in 1958) and received his doctorate from [[Princeton University]] in 1963. He then went to [[Cornell University]], where he became assistant professor in 1966 and associate professor in 1969. In 1970 he became Associate Professor and in 1976 Professor at the [[College of William & Mary|College of William and Mary]]. From 1996 to 2000 he was Dean of Research (and Graduate Studies) there and in 2002 he retired.

He has also worked at the particle accelerator CEBAF (later the [[Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility]], JLAB), from 1984 as associate director for Research, from 1986 as Senior Staff Theorist and from 2000 to 2002 as interim Head of the Theory Department and then as Principal Staff Scientist.

He has been a visiting scientist at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] (1969), the [[Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare|INFN (Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare)]] in Rome (1989), the [[Utrecht University|University of Utrecht]] (1990), the Institute for Nuclear Theory (INT) at the [[University of Washington]] and a visiting professor at [[Carnegie Mellon University|Carnegie-Mellon University]] (1981) and the Leibniz University of Hannover (1983). He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and was a Fulbright and Woodrow Wilson Fellow.

==Research==

Gross's work included the relativistic [[Few-body systems|few-body problem]] in [[Nuclear physics|nuclear]] and [[particle physics]] (for example, [[quark|quark models]] of [[mesons]] or [[nucleons]] in the [[deuteron]] or [[helium-3]]),<ref>{{cite journal|author= Franz Gross  |name-list-style=amp |title=Relativistic few-body problem. I. Two-body equations |journal=Phys. Rev. C |year=1982|volume=26|  issue=5 |page=2203 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.26.2203 |bibcode=1982PhRvC..26.2203G }}</ref> the electromagnetic structure of hadrons and nuclei (elastic and inelastic [[electron scattering]])<ref>{{cite journal|author1=R. Gilman|author2=Franz Gross  |name-list-style=amp |title=Electromagnetic structure of the deuteron |journal= J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. |year=2002|volume=28|  issue=4 |page=R37|doi=10.1088/0954-3899/28/4/201|arxiv=nucl-th/0111015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Raymond G. Arnold  |author2=Carl E. Carlson|author3= Franz Gross  |name-list-style=amp |title=Polarization transfer in elastic electron scattering from nucleons and deuterons |journal=Phys. Rev. C |year=1981|volume=23 |  issue=1 |page=363 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.23.363|bibcode=1981PhRvC..23..363A |osti=1445684 }}</ref> and relativistic wave equations for bound states.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Franz Gross  |name-list-style=amp |title=Three-Dimensional Covariant Integral Equations for Low-Energy Systems |journal=Phys. Rev. C |year=1969|volume=186|  issue=5 |page=1448|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.186.1448|bibcode=1969PhRv..186.1448G }}</ref> He wrote a textbook on quantum field theory.
